title: Lamrim: the round of suffering
hookLine: the faults of samsara, seen plainly

cards: The dishwasher clicks off. Everything comes out clean and goes back in the cupboard. By dinner the sink is full again, and it all starts over.
Nobody did anything wrong; that's just how dishes work. Now stretch that out. The craving that gets fed and comes back hungrier.
The same argument with the same person, in nearly the same words, one more time. A new phone, thrilling on Monday and ordinary by the weekend.
The lamrim asks the student to stop here and look at the whole machine, plainly, without flinching.

teach.b: First, the name for the machine. Samsara, in Sanskrit, usually translated as wandering on. Tibetans call it khorwa, circling.
In this teaching it's the round of birth, death and birth again, driven by craving and confusion, life after life.
Second, the faults. The lamrim texts lay them out plainly. Nothing in the circle stays certain: friends become strangers, the high fall low, fortunes turn.
Nothing in it satisfies for long: the more you drink of it, the thirstier you get. And it keeps happening, with no natural end in sight. Third, a picture from the older suttas.

teach.h: MORE TEARS THAN THE FOUR OCEANS.
teach.b: In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha asks his monks which is greater: the tears they have shed while wandering on through this long round, weeping over what they lost and what they couldn't have, or the water in the four great oceans.
The answer in the text is the tears. Fourth, why look at all this. Tibetan teachers say you can't want to leave a place you haven't seen clearly.

teach.h: SEEING IT PLAINLY: THE WISH TO BE FREE.
teach.b: Seeing the round plainly gives rise to renunciation, the honest wish to be free. That isn't hatred of life. Lunch is still good.
A friend's laugh is still good. What the student turns away from is the circling itself, getting caught again and again. Yesterday was karma, the engine; today is the road it runs on.
If your own tears feel like too much to carry, you don't have to carry them alone: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

how: In the Tibetan stages-of-the-path teaching, students reflect on the faults of samsara so that renunciation, the wish to be free of the round, grows strong before they turn to the later stages.

o: the next stair: learning to hate this life and leave it
the next stair: a wheel that turns toward a happy end
the next stair: seeing samsara plainly enough to want out

games.q: the round of suffering: tap the pairs.
p: wandering on, the round of rebirth
less water than the tears shed
the honest wish to be free

s: seeing the faults of samsara means hating life
teachers say it's the circling the student turns from, not friends, laughter or lunch.
in a sutta, the Buddha compares tears shed while wandering on to the four great oceans
the text says the tears are more.
the lamrim keeps the faults of samsara vague
it names them plainly: no certainty, no lasting satisfaction, and it keeps happening.

games.q: you've noticed the same loop in your life for the hundredth time. what does this stage of the lamrim ask of you first?
o: look at it plainly, all the way around.
games.why: the teaching asks for clear seeing first. teachers say the wish to be free grows from seeing the round plainly, not from shame.

practice: Let one loop in your life come to mind: checking the phone, the same worry at three in the morning, the same apology.
Without judging or fixing it, trace it once around, what starts it, what feeds it, what it promises, how it ends up back where it began, and give it a short, plain name.
Then rest with the breath, which also goes round and round, and asks nothing of you.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim. The stages of the path. Today's stage: seeing samsara, the round of suffering, plainly enough to want out. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: samsara, the round of birth and death; in Tibetan, khorwa (འཁོར་བ), circling.

carryVoice: Your line: round and round. Seeing the circle plainly is where the wish to be free begins. Same time tomorrow.
